opening: In a newly settled village in Meiji-era Japan, a father finds a brown bear eating his only daughter in the forest. He shoots it and weeps over her remains. Knowing these wary bears rarely attack unfamiliar living humans, he nevertheless fears other villagers will also suffer having relatives eaten. Why?
solution: Days earlier an epidemic killed his daughter and several villagers. The new settlement lacked a crematorium and could not spare enough fuel, so their bodies were buried in the forest. On his daily visit to her grave, he discovered that a bear had dug her up and eaten her remains. He feared other bears would raid the graves and eat other families' dead relatives; he was not predicting attacks on living people.

rubric.criterion: Daughter and other villagers died days earlier in an epidemic, before any bear feeding.
Lack of crematorium/fuel in new settlement led to forest burial; father found disturbed grave during his regular visit.
Bear dug up and ate corpse; he shot it, but worried other bears could raid other graves and distress relatives, not kill living villagers.
